intro: Enschede's old trees were bought by textile money. Van Heek, Blijdenstein, Ledeboer: the families who ran the mills built estates on the edge of town, hired the best garden architects in the country and planted them, and the city later absorbed the results as public parks. One invoice survives. In 1865 D. Wattez billed H. J. van Heek for a Wellingtonia as part of the planting around 't Wageler, and the two men wrote to each other about the price. That giant sequoia is still standing in the Ledeboerpark, which is the closest thing this page has to a receipt.
meta_description: Twelve remarkable trees in Enschede: a giant sequoia with a surviving 1865 invoice, two on an estate first recorded in 1536, and an oak in a city square.
question_meta: Enschede's oldest tree is the oak on 't Zeggelt, banded 1750 to 1800 by the national register. Where it stands, and eleven more worth the walk.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Enschede is the oak on 't Zeggelt, in the Lasonder-Zeggelt district, which the national register places in a planting band of 1750 to 1800, so between about 225 and 275 years old. It has a name of its own in the city, De Eik op 't Zeggelt, and it stands in public planting rather than on any estate, which is unusual here: almost every other old tree in Enschede is a survivor of a nineteenth century textile family's grounds. The register gives it a coordinate to six decimal places, which is the sort of precision that means somebody stood at the trunk with a receiver rather than pointing at an address.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every age on this page is a band and none is narrowed to look precise. The register is the 2024 edition and is the single source for these trees, which is why they are all flagged. The giant sequoia in the Ledeboerpark is the exception worth naming: the register cites a document in the archive of the Twente textile families recording correspondence in 1866 between H. J. van Heek and the garden architect D. Wattez about the price of a Wellingtonia, on an invoice for planting around 't Wageler in 1865. That is a documented purchase rather than an estimate, and it is why this page can be more confident about that tree than about any other on it. Where a pin is marked approximate we know the grounds and not the trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Enschede?
faq.a: De Eik op 't Zeggelt, in the Lasonder-Zeggelt district, banded 1750 to 1800 by the national register.

faq.q: Is there really an invoice for one of these trees?
faq.a: The register cites one. A document in the archive of the Twente textile families records that in 1866 H. J. van Heek and the garden architect D. Wattez corresponded about the price of a Wellingtonia on an invoice for planting around 't Wageler in 1865. Wellingtonia is the old trade name for the giant sequoia, and one from that period still stands in the Ledeboerpark, which grew out of that estate.

faq.q: Can you get onto Landgoed Het Bouwhuis?
faq.a: Yes. The register records the grounds as open to the public and notes that a good many striking trees stand there. Het Bouwhuis and the neighbouring Het Amelink appear in writing as early as 1536, when Jan van Borne, steward of the chapter of St Peter in Utrecht, reported on both farms in the hamlet of Lonneker.
All seven. The Ledeboerpark, the Blijdensteinpark and Het Bouwhuis are open, and the oak, the plane and the Wageler beech stand on public ground.

trees.name: The Wellingtonia of the Ledeboerpark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 155 to 165 years, and the register cites an 1865 invoice for a Wellingtonia planted here
trees.story:
Somebody wrote down what this tree cost.

The register cites a document in the archive of the Twente textile families: in 1866 the mill owner H. J. van Heek and the garden architect D. Wattez corresponded about the price of a Wellingtonia, itemised on an invoice for the planting around 't Wageler in 1865. Wellingtonia was the trade name the British gave the giant sequoia after the Duke of Wellington, and in the 1860s it was the most fashionable and most expensive thing you could put in a garden in Europe. The species had only been introduced to Britain in 1853. Buying one was a way of saying what you were worth.

The park is what became of that estate. Wattez laid it out in the second half of the nineteenth century, the city absorbed it, and the Ledeboerpark on the Hengelosestraat is now open to anyone.

So you can go and stand under an object of Victorian conspicuous consumption that has quietly outlived the mills, the family's fortune and the argument about the price.

It is unmistakable: the thick red-brown trunk with soft fibrous bark, and a straight conical top.
trees.transport: About 2 km northwest of Enschede station, on the Hengelosestraat.

trees.how_to_recognise: The single huge conifer with spongy red-brown bark and a conical crown.

trees.name: De Eik op 't Zeggelt
trees.age_estimate: roughly 225 to 275 years, from the register's planting band of 1750 to 1800
trees.story:
The oldest tree in Enschede is not on anybody's estate. It stands in ordinary public planting in a residential district and it has a name anyway, which is usually a sign that people have been walking past it long enough to need one.

The register bands it 1750 to 1800, which makes it two to two and a half centuries and puts its first decades in a Twente of farms and hand looms, before the mills, before the railway, and long before the town around it. Enschede burned almost entirely to the ground in 1862, when a fire took the whole centre in a few hours. This oak was standing well outside it and is one of the few living things in the city that predates that day.

The register gives its position to six decimal places, which is the tell that somebody stood at the trunk with a satellite receiver rather than pointing at a street. That is unusual in this dataset and it means the pin is as good as pins get.

Pedunculate oak, so acorns on long stalks and leaves that sit almost directly on the twig. In October there will be a great many of them underfoot.
trees.access: Free. Public planting in a residential district, reachable at any time.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km north of Enschede station, in the Lasonder-Zeggelt district.
trees.how_to_recognise: A single very heavy old oak standing clear in the green of the district, far thicker than anything near it.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns are down

trees.name: The Beech of Landgoed Wageler
trees.age_estimate: roughly 185 to 195 years, from the register's planting band of 1830 to 1840
trees.story:
This beech was on the estate before the estate was designed.

't Wageler is the ground that Wattez planted for the Van Heeks in the 1860s and that partly became the Ledeboerpark. The register bands this tree 1830 to 1840, thirty years earlier, which means it was a mature tree of some size when the landscape architect arrived with his plans and his invoices.

That is the ordinary way a Dutch estate garden was actually made. You did not clear ground and start over. You looked at what was standing, kept whatever was good, and arranged the new planting to make the most of it, which is why the oldest tree in a nineteenth century park is so often older than the park.

It stands along the Es, the old open arable field that these Twente farms were organised around. An es is a very specific thing here: a slightly raised field built up over centuries by carting in sods and manure, so the soil under it can be a metre deeper than the heath beside it. Good ground, and part of why a beech here grew as it did.

Smooth grey bark, deep shade, bare litter beneath.
trees.access: Free. On the estate grounds, recorded as visitable in the national register.
trees.transport: About 2.5 km northwest of Enschede station, near the Ledeboerpark.
trees.how_to_recognise: A heavy smooth-barked beech standing along the edge of the old open field.

best_time.label: October, when the whole crown goes copper

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of Het Bouwhuis
trees.age_estimate: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.story:
The farm this tree stands on was first written down in 1536.

In that year Jan van Borne, steward of the chapter of St Peter in Utrecht, reported on two holdings in the hamlet of Lonneker: Het Bouwhuis and Het Amelink. The Amelink then belonged to the Jonker van Steinfurt, which is to say the count of Bentheim. So the ground has an unbroken paper trail running back close to five centuries, into a landscape of church chapters and minor German nobility, which is roughly four hundred years before anyone here had heard of a sequoia.

The tree is the newcomer, planted somewhere between 1900 and 1910, when a giant sequoia had gone from a spectacular novelty to the standard way of announcing that a country house had grounds.

The register notes that Het Bouwhuis is open to the public and that a good many striking trees stand there, which makes this one of the easier estates on this page to simply walk into.

A hundred and twenty years is nothing for the species. In California this would be a sapling among trees three thousand years old. Here it is already the biggest thing in the field.
trees.access: Free. The register records the grounds as open to the public.
trees.transport: About 5 km northeast of Enschede station, at Lonneker.
trees.how_to_recognise: The tall conical conifer with thick spongy red-brown bark, well clear of the other trees.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech by the Pond
trees.age_estimate: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910

location.address: Landgoed Het Bouwhuis, northeast side of the pond, Lonneker

trees.story:
Go inside it. That is the point of a weeping beech and almost nobody does it.

The branches of a mature one arch out and then fall straight to the ground all the way round, so what you have is a green tent perhaps fifteen metres across with a bare floor and a trunk in the middle. Children work this out immediately. Adults walk past.

Weeping beech is a cultivar, not a species: a mutant form propagated by grafting, so every one is a clone of an original found in Europe in the eighteenth century. The graft union is usually visible as a swelling low on the trunk. It grows the same way a normal beech does except that it cannot hold its branches up, and left alone it will layer, meaning a branch resting on soil roots and becomes a new trunk, so an old one can slowly walk outward across a lawn.

This one stands on the northeast side of the pond at Het Bouwhuis, planted between 1900 and 1910, on ground documented since 1536.

Duck under the skirt on the pond side and look back out at the water through the leaves.
trees.access: Free. The register records the grounds as open to the public.
trees.transport: About 5 km northeast of Enschede station, at Lonneker.
trees.how_to_recognise: A dome of branches falling to the grass beside the pond, hollow inside.

trees.name: The Sessile Oak of the Blijdensteinpark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910

location.address: Blijdensteinpark, east side by the filling station

trees.story:
A dual carriageway runs through this park, and the tree is by a filling station. Both facts are worth stating first, because they are what this place is now.

It began as an estate. In 1855 H. G. Blijdenstein and his wife Ebeling built a villa on the Helweg, the road that later became the Gronausestraat, and laid out grounds around it. Their daughter Johanna Ida Beltman-Blijdenstein was the last person to live there. The Blijdensteins were one of the Twente textile dynasties, and like the Van Heeks and the Ledeboers what they left the city was ground with trees on it.

What happened afterwards is what happens to green space near a growing city. The Boulevard 1945 was driven straight through the park, cutting it in two, and the eastern edge now holds a petrol station.

The oak has been there since around 1900 to 1910 and has watched the arrangement change around it. It is a sessile oak, so the acorns sit tight against the twig and the leaves have a clear stalk, the reverse of the commoner pedunculate oak.

Go on a Sunday, when the road is quiet.
trees.transport: About 2 km east of Enschede station, on the Boulevard 1945.
trees.how_to_recognise: On the east side of the park near the filling station, with acorns sitting tight to the twig.

trees.name: The Plane of 't Zwik
trees.age_estimate: roughly 155 to 165 years, from the register's planting band of 1860 to 1870

location.address: Cort van der Lindelaan, near the Tubantiasingel

trees.story:
There was a country house here called 't Zwik and there is a street pattern instead.

The city bought the place in 1917 to expand into, and built over it through the 1920s and 1930s, which was the ordinary fate of the smaller estates on the edge of a town whose population was climbing with every new mill. The house went. What survived is planting: this plane, and, sixty to a hundred metres to the west, an oak and a beech that the register also identifies as remnants of the same grounds.

That is a useful thing to know while standing here. Three trees at three points along a street are not a coincidence, they are the last legible trace of a garden, and if you draw a line between them you are walking somebody's approach.

The plane is the easiest of the three to spot: flaking bark in cream, olive and grey, big maple-shaped leaves, and the bristly round seed balls that hang on through the winter.

Planes are the great survivors of city building. They tolerate compacted soil, root disturbance, pollution and hard pruning better than anything else of their size, which is exactly why this one is still here and the house is not.
trees.access: Free. Street tree on public ground.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km west of Enschede station, on the Cort van der Lindelaan.
trees.how_to_recognise: Camouflage-patterned flaking bark, near the Tubantiasingel end of the street.

trees.name: The Hungarian Oak of the Oosterbegraafplaats
trees.age_estimate: roughly 100 years, from a registered planting date around 1930

location.address: Oosterbegraafplaats, northern main path, Noord Esmarkerrondweg 407, Enschede

trees.access: Free. The cemetery is a public rijksmonument, open daily from sunrise to sunset.
trees.transport: About 3 km northeast of Enschede city centre (Noord Esmarkerrondweg 407); best reached by bicycle or car. No specific bus line verified this pass.
trees.story:
The register does not only call this oak old, it says which decade of the cemetery it belongs to. Gedenkpark De Ooster opened in 1899, its northern section was added in 1929, and the Bomenstichting dates this Hungarian oak to that extension, which puts it at roughly a hundred years. The register throws in one detail worth having on the walk: the seam between the old ground and the new is still legible in the layout, and this tree stands on the new side of it.

Quercus frainetto belongs to southern Italy, the Balkans and Thrace. In a cemetery in Twente it is a deliberate import, and somebody chose it over the beeches and oaks that would have been the easy answer. It has grown here through everything that has happened to Enschede since 1930: the war, the slow closing of the textile mills that paid for this city, and the rebuilding of a town that had to find something else to be.

The ground around it is a national monument in its own right, protected in part for the park trees along these paths, though that listing praises them as a group and does not name this oak. The tree register does, and it is the only source that does, so read the dating as the register's judgement rather than as a count anybody has taken from the wood.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, far bigger and more deeply cut than the native oaks here. It stands on the northern main path, in the 1929 part of the cemetery, on the new side of the seam between the old ground and the new.

trees.name: The Sweet Gum of the Oosterbegraafplaats
trees.age_estimate: roughly 90 years, from a registered planting date around 1935

location.address: Oosterbegraafplaats, northern main path (second section, right side), Noord Esmarkerrondweg 407, Enschede

trees.access: Free. The cemetery is a public rijksmonument, open daily from sunrise to sunset.
trees.transport: About 3 km northeast of Enschede city centre (Noord Esmarkerrondweg 407); best reached by bicycle or car. No specific bus line verified this pass.
trees.story:
This tree is on the national register for being a good example of its species, not an old one. The Bomenstichting dates the planting to around 1935, give or take five years, and listed it on dendrological grounds: a fine sweet gum, in a country where the species is a garden import rather than a native.

Liquidambar styraciflua comes from the wet bottomlands of the American southeast. What it does in autumn is the whole reason anyone plants it here. The leaves are shaped like five-pointed stars and they refuse to turn one colour: scarlet, plum, orange and green show up on the same branch, sometimes on the same leaf, and the display runs on for weeks after the limes and beeches around it have gone brown and let go.

It stands on the second stretch of the northern main path, in a cemetery that calls itself a memorial park and means it. Gedenkpark De Ooster opened in 1899 and is now a national monument, protected in part for the trees along its paths, which is how an American swamp tree ends up growing old in Twente with nothing much asked of it.

Only the tree register names this specimen individually, so the planting date is its estimate rather than a documented year.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, five-pointed stars like a maple's but set singly along the twig, and by the corky ridges on its shoots. It stands on the right of the northern main path, on its second stretch.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the star-shaped leaves go scarlet and plum at once

trees.name: The Oriental Spruce of the Oosterbegraafplaats
trees.access: Free. The cemetery is a public rijksmonument, open daily from sunrise to sunset.
trees.transport: About 3 km northeast of Enschede city centre (Noord Esmarkerrondweg 407); best reached by bicycle or car. No specific bus line verified this pass.
trees.story:
Nobody has dated this spruce, and age is not why it is protected. The Bomenstichting listed it on dendrological grounds: Picea orientalis is a tree of the Caucasus and the mountains of northeast Turkey, uncommon in this corner of the Netherlands, and this is a good one.

It is the easiest spruce in Europe to identify by hand. Oriental spruce carries the shortest needles of any spruce, blunt at the tip rather than sharp, dark and glossy and packed tight all round the shoot, so the whole tree reads denser and blacker than the Norway spruces Dutch planters reached for by default. In its own range it covers the wet Black Sea slopes in forest up to the tree line. Here it stands in a cemetery on the eastern edge of Enschede, about fifty metres from a Hungarian oak, in ground laid out as a memorial park in 1899 and now a national monument.

How it got here is not written down. The register's age field says unknown, and rather than put a number on it we have left it empty: a spruce can look venerable at eighty and ordinary at two hundred, and guessing would be the easy kind of dishonesty.

If you know when this one went in, or have seen a planting record for the northern section, tell us and we will date it properly.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the needles, the shortest of any spruce and blunt rather than sharp, dark and packed tight all round the shoot. It stands about fifty metres from the Hungarian oak, off the northern path.

trees.name: The Silver Lime of Stroinksbleekweg
trees.age_estimate: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890

location.address: Corner of Stroinksbleekweg and Hulsmaatstraat, Roombeek, Enschede

trees.access: Free. Stands in a public street-side green strip (plantsoen), no restriction.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Enschede city centre / Enschede railway station, in the Roombeek district; walkable.
trees.story:
A silver lime has held this street corner since the 1880s and nobody wrote down why. The Bomenstichting register puts the planting between 1880 and 1890, which makes the tree roughly 140 years old, designates it monumental, and then leaves its history field blank. It is also the only source that names this tree at all.

Tilia tomentosa is the lime you notice in wind. Its leaves are dark green on top and coated underneath in fine white felt, so a gust turns the whole crown silver and then back again. It also flowers weeks after every other lime in the street, in high summer, with a scent that reaches you before the tree does.

The corner is in Roombeek, the district rebuilt after the fireworks depot went up on 13 May 2000, killing 23 people, injuring around 950 and flattening hundreds of homes. The blast site is roughly a kilometre south of here. What happened on this corner that afternoon is not recorded in anything we have been able to find, and assuming an old tree survived a disaster because it is old and standing is exactly the kind of tidy story that turns out to be wrong. If you were here, or know what this corner looked like that week, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in any breeze: the leaves are dark above and white-felted underneath, so the whole crown flashes silver. It stands on the corner of Stroinksbleekweg and Hulsmaatstraat, about thirty metres from the old elm.

best_time.label: late July, when it comes into flower weeks after the other limes and you smell it before you see it

trees.name: The Dutch Elm of Stroinksbleekweg
trees.age_estimate: roughly 140 years, from a registered planting date around 1890
trees.access: Free. Stands in a public park strip, no restriction.
trees.transport: About 1 km north of Enschede city centre / Enschede railway station, in the Roombeek district; walkable, about 30m from the Silver Lime of Stroinksbleekweg (ens_011).
trees.story:
A full-grown elm in a Dutch street is rarer than it looks. The disease that carries the country's name was first described here in the 1920s, named after the Dutch pathologists who worked it out rather than after the tree, and it went on to kill the great majority of the elms in the Netherlands. This one, which the Bomenstichting register dates to between 1880 and 1890, is still standing.

Ulmus x hollandica is a cross between wych elm and field elm, and it was the workhorse tree of the Low Countries: planted along dykes, quays and town streets by the thousand because it tolerates wind, salt and heavy clay. Most of that planting is gone. The survivors tend to be single trees in odd corners rather than the avenues they were meant to be.

The register gives this elm the same 1880 to 1890 band as the silver lime about thirty metres away and calls both monumental. Whether the two went in together is not recorded; the history field for each of them is blank, and the register is the only source that names either. The pair make a short stop about a kilometre north of Enschede station, on the edge of Roombeek, where almost everything else on the street is newer than they are.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, rough as sandpaper and lopsided where they meet the stalk, one side of the base set lower than the other. It stands about thirty metres from the silver lime on the same corner.
